# Part 1 - Reproducible Report and Data Description
## 1.1 Introduction

For this homework, I have selected the Student Performance dataset. 
This dataset uses a response variable of Final Score, with three predictors: the amount of study hours per week,
the students attendance as a percentage, and the students prior score. The goal of this homework is to fit and
diagnose a linear model using matrix computation.

## 1.2 Data Inspection and Validation

```{python}
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("data/data_raw/student_performance.csv")

print(data.head())
print("shape:", data.shape)
print("data types:", data.dtypes)
```

The first five raws of data are `{python} data.head()`

The shape of the data is `{python} data.shape`

The data types of the data are `{python} pd.DataFrame(data.dtypes)`

The amount of missing values per column are `{python} pd.DataFrame(data.isna().sum())`

Are the ID's in the id column unique: `{python} data["id"].is_unique`

There is one response variable (the final_score column), with three predictor variables (study_hours_per_week,
attendance_pct, prior_score). There are a total of 120 observations and there are no missing values in any of the
columns. The IDs are also unique.

# Part 2 - Matrix Setup and Standardization

Convert the predictors and response to NumPy arrays
```{python}
import numpy as np

predictors = data[
    ["study_hours_per_week", "attendance_pct", "prior_score"]
].to_numpy()

y = data["final_score"].to_numpy()
```

Standardize the predictors
```{python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (
    predictors - means
) / sds

Z.mean(axis=0), Z.std(axis=0)
```

Construct the design matrix
```{python}
X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(Z)),
    Z
])
```

The shape of predictors is `{python} predictors.shape`

The shape of Z is `{python} Z.shape`

The shape of X is `{python} X.shape`

The shape of y is `{python} y.shape`

The rank of X is `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`

The number of predictors is 1 less than the rank of X: `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) - 1)`

X and y must have compatible shapes because otherwise matrix operations (such as addition or multiplication) between
them wouldn't work. We include the intercept column in the X matrix because that will tell us what the
$\widehat{\beta_0}$ that we calculate will be. Standardizing the predictors was done so that we can more easily
compare the distribution to a normal distribution, with the standardized predictors now reporting how many standard
deviations away from the mean they are. Broadcasting made this standardization possible with out a Python loop because
in the Z calculation, it was implied that each element in the predictors array was to be subtracted by the mean of that
row, so a loop was not needed to iterate through each element in the predictors array individually. The same is true
for dividing by the sds of each row. It was implied that each element in the (predictors - mean) array was to be
divided by the sds, so a loop iterating through each element is not needed.

# Part 3 - Least Squares

Fit the model:
```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)

beta_hat
```

The intercept of this model is approximately `{python} round(float(beta_hat[0]), 4)` points of final score

The coefficient of the standardized study hours per week predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[1]), 4)`

The coefficient of the standardized attendance percentage predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[2]), 4)`

The coefficient of the standarized prior score predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[3]), 4)`

Out of the three standardized predictors, prior score has the largest absolute value coefficient

Calculate fitted values:
```{python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
```

Calculate residuals:
```{python}
residuals = y - fitted
```

The mean of the residuals is approximately `{python} round(float(residuals.mean()), 5)`

And the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is approximately:
```{python}
rmse = np.sqrt(
    np.mean(
        residuals ** 2
    )
)

round(float(rmse), 4)
```

X @ beta_hat represents our approximation of the response values given the predictor values. So X @ beta_hat
gives us the y_hat values, which are the y-values of our linear regression model. The residual mean should be near
zero when an intercept is present because the residuals measure how far off from our prediction model the actual
measured values are, and for a normal distribution the residuals should have equal variance and have a mean of
0. The Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE) summarizes the square root of the average squared distance between the actual
measured values and the predicted values, and this is helpful as it returns an error in the original units of the
response variable. The difference between X @ beta_hat and X * beta_hat is that the @ operator is matrix
multiplication, whereas the * operator signifies element wise mutliplication. So the * operator multiplies
each element of X with the same element of beta_hat, but that is not the matrix multiplication that we want for this
operation. We want mathematical matrix multiplication, which uses the @ symbol.

# Part 4 - QR, SVD, and conditioning

QR decomposition:
```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)

print("Shape of Q:", Q.shape)
print("Shape of R:", R.shape)

print("Q @ R = X:",
np.allclose(
    Q @ R,
    X
))

print("Q.T @ Q = I:",
np.allclose(
    Q.T @ Q,
    np.eye(Q.shape[1])
))
```

Single Value Decomposition (SVD):
```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(
    X,
    full_matrices=False
)
```

The shape of U is: `{python} U.shape`

The shape of s is: `{python} s.shape`

The shape of Vt is: `{python} Vt.shape`

The singular values are `{python} s`

Reconstruct X:
```{python}
X_reconstructed = (
    U
    @ np.diag(s)
    @ Vt
)

print("X_reconstructed = X:",
np.allclose(
    X_reconstructed,
    X
))
```

Rank and conditioning:

The rank of X is `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`

The condition number of X is approximately `{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X)), 4)`

Raw, unstandardized design matrix:
```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(predictors)),
    predictors
])
```

The condition number of the raw, unstandardized data is approximately
`{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X_raw)), 4)`

Q @ R $\approx$ X verifies that the design matrix X has been correctly decomposed into the components of Q and R,
and when Q and R are matrix multiplied back together, they should gives us back (approximately because of
computational rounding) our design matrix X. Q.T @ Q $\approx$ I verifies that the matrix Q is an orthonormal matrix,
because for an orthonormal matrix Q, Q.t @ Q = I, so this is just verifying that that is true, because the QR
decomposition should return Q as an orthonormal matrix. The singular values from SVD tell us which directions are
stronger and weaker in regards to the predictors effect on the response. Higher singular values mean a stronger effect
on the response, and lower singular values mean a weaker effect on the response. A large condition number suggests
that there is some collinearity betweent the predictors, so there might be some redundancy in the information provided
by the predictors. For this data, the condition number did very drastically change after standardization. This happened
because the condition number is based on the largest singular value and the smallest singular value. And this will
be affected by the scaling of the units between predictors. If one predictor is measured in the thousands, and another
is measured in single digits, the condition number will be very large. The condition number being very large is more due
to scale mismatching between predictors, more than it is about collinearity in that case. So that is why we used a
standardized design matrix, so that all the predictors had very similar scales for their measurements, which means that
the condition number here tells us more about whether any predictors are colinear or not. Based on this, the
standardized design matrix does not show any evidence of sever-near redundancy among predictors, as the condition
number for the design matrix was `{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X)),4)`, which is fairly close to 1.

# Part 5 - Reproducibility and Numerical Computing Reflection

Clean execution matters a lot for a computational report as it is very important that your work is reproducible
so that others can verify your work and hopefully get the same result everytime, and so that others can also
build off of your work and be sure that there are no problems with it. This is why it is also important that 
reusable code not depend on hidden notebook states, as that would make the whole report not reproducible as 
important variables or code would depend on something that is specific to only you and no one else.
The reason np.linalg.lstsq() is preferable to manually computing $(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$ is because computing inverses 
takes a lot of computational power, and that can make the process very slow and resource intensive, especially 
for larger datasets, whereas the least squares method is much easier to run and can save a lot of time and resources, 
especially for larger datasets. For checking the results from SVD and QR decomposition, np.allclose() is preferable 
to using exact equalities because there is often computational rounding involved, so the result is approximately
(within very small tolerances) equal, but often not exactly equal, even though they are equal for our purposes. The 
condition number comparison taught me that the scale of measurements between predictors matters, and can give you a 
falsely large condition number, even if the predictors have almost no collinearity. One reproducibility practice from
this homework that I will carry into the final project is making sure that code runs sequentially from top to bottom,
and making sure that everything runs from top to bottom without issue with a refreshed kernel so that I am sure that 
there are no hidden notebook states.
